summary.text: For \(n=67\), the two distinct integers \(147\) and \(2055\) both give residue sums equal to \(67\): respectively \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19\) and \(1+3+9\cdot 7\). Thus the multiplicity at \(67\) is at least two, contradicting the claimed value of one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k),
\]
so that A049802 has value \(F(m)\) at index \(m\). For a positive integer \(n\), the function used in the conjecture is
\[
a(n)=\#\{m\in\mathbb N:0\le m<2^{n+1}\text{ and }F(m)=n\}.
\]
(The bound \(2^{n+1}\) is the stipulated sufficient search bound for occurrences of the positive value \(n\).) We will disprove the assertion that \(a(n)=1\) for every
\[
n\in S=\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}
\]
by showing that \(a(67)\ge 2\).

Consider first \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). Thus the residue sum defining \(F(147)\) has exactly the seven terms corresponding to the moduli \(2,4,8,16,32,64,128\). These residues are
\[
\begin{aligned}
147\bmod 2&=1,\\
147\bmod 4&=3,\\
147\bmod 8&=3,\\
147\bmod 16&=3,\\
147\bmod 32&=19,\\
147\bmod 64&=19,\\
147\bmod 128&=19.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, \(147=144+3\), which gives remainder \(3\) modulo \(4,8,16\); and \(147=128+19\), with \(19<32\), which gives remainder \(19\) modulo \(32,64,128\). Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=10+57=67.
\]

Now consider \(m=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Also
\[
2055=2048+7=2^{11}+7.
\]
For every \(k\) with \(3\le k\le11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}\), while \(7<2^k\). Hence
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7\qquad(3\le k\le11).
\]
For the two smaller powers we have
\[
2055\bmod2=1,\qquad 2055\bmod4=3.
\]
There are nine integers \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\), inclusive. Therefore
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=4+63=67.
\]
Thus \(67\) occurs in A049802 at both indices \(147\) and \(2055\).

Both indices are included in the finite set used to define \(a(67)\). Indeed,
\[
147<2055<2^{12}\le2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
Moreover, \(147\ne2055\). Hence the set
\[
\{m\in\mathbb N: m<2^{68}\text{ and }F(m)=67\}
\]
contains at least the two distinct elements \(147\) and \(2055\). Its cardinality is therefore at least two, so
\[
a(67)\ge2,
\]
and in particular \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\in S\). The conjecture would therefore imply \(a(67)=1\), contradicting the inequality \(a(67)\ge2\) just proved. Consequently it is false that \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n\in\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}\).
